items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He was a songwriter, mostly. Basie’s playing was very much in that style... what was that thing that Neal Hefty [phonetic] did for him?

ctx.x: He was a songwriter, mostly. Basie’s playing was very much in that style, and very good in that style, which I think we haven’t heard too much of other than . . . oh, what was that thing that Neal Hefty [phonetic] did for him? The Kid from Red Bank, where he played some real strides, you know. But it certainly showed that he was well versed in that style.

While we’re discussing these Harlem stride players, maybe we could go through several of them that I happened to just job down that you could give us your impressions of or reminiscences about. We mentioned Willy “The Lion” and his relationship to you. Fats Waller, you just brought up, and when did you get to know him?

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I know that Neal Hefty was invited out there... I know Dick Klein was telling me that... he just picked up a phone one day and called Neal Hefty

ctx.x: But of course that's just one particular case.

That's one particular case, but of course I know that Neal Hefty was invited out there under somewhat similar circumstances, not by any instigation of mine, but I know Dick Klein was telling me that when, I believe it was "Sex and the Single Girl" ... he wanted that sound that Hefty had been getting, you know, with the Basie thing, and he just picked up a phone one day and called Neal Hefty in New York, and said, "How would you like to come out and work on a picture for me?" It was just like that, and he came --…
The Hollywood work goes on and off; I mean, it isn't something like a band where you're doing something every day and it's just a question of getting an assignment, so all this time ...
